description: LunarLink is a multidisciplinary space-tech team combining astronomy, physics, and software to make complex lunar mission data simple, visual, and actionable. Our goal is to help explore and compare lunar south-pole landing opportunities through Sun, Earth, lighting, and communication analysis.
summary:
At the Moon's south pole the Sun never climbs; it circles the horizon, so a single ridge can mean days of darkness and a dead battery. When a launch slips by even a few days, a landing site that was safe can become fatal, and planners must redo the analysis under pressure.

LunarLink_JO answers that question in seconds. The user chooses a site, a landing day, a mission length and a lander. The tool returns a one-sentence verdict, shows why, and proposes the nearest date or site that still works. Our "Ring of Light" draws a full month of sunlight, Earth contact and lander state in one circle.

Every number comes from NASA open data: LOLA terrain, the SPICE ephemeris, Moon Mineralogy Mapper ice detections and Lunar Prospector chemistry. It also checks slope, the nearest water ice and a rover route to reach it. The site runs in any browser, in Arabic and English.
details:
LunarLink_JO is a web tool that answers one question a lunar mission planner asks under pressure: the launch slipped, is our landing site still good?

What it does and how it works

The user sets one plan: a landing site, a landing day, a mission length (1 to 60 days) and a lander (battery, power load, solar panels). LunarLink_JO returns a one-sentence verdict (the mission works, the lander sleeps, or the lander is lost) and shows why in five tabs:

  • Overview: the verdict and the “Ring of Light”, our own way of drawing a whole month of sunlight, Earth contact and lander state in one circle.
  • Sky and map: the real 360° terrain horizon around the site with the Sun and Earth moving on it, plus a 3D Moon where any point can be clicked and analysed.
  • Sites and dates: every candidate site compared across dates, so a slipped schedule can be re-checked in seconds. If the plan fails, the tool proposes the nearest landing date or the nearest site that still works.
  • Power: an hour-by-hour battery simulation with a sleep mode, and the best direction to point the solar panels.
  • Rocks, slope and ice: estimated rock types around the site, slope statistics inside the landing circle, the nearest water-ice regions, and a rover route to the ice that avoids slopes above a limit the user chooses.

Behind the screen, the tool casts 2,880 rays from each site out to 300 km over the curved Moon to build the terrain horizon. Sunlight is the fraction of the Sun’s disc visible above that horizon, computed every hour. Earth contact is line of sight to the Earth. The lander is modelled as an hourly energy balance.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Mission planners can re-check a site and a date in seconds when a schedule moves, instead of reading tables of raw angles.
  • Science and engineering teams look at light, communication, power, slope and ice for the same plan in one shared view.
  • Educators and students get a built-in guide that explains every calculation, with formulas and references. The whole site is in Arabic and English, which opens it to classrooms across the Arab region.

The tool already produces findings: around one of our candidate points on the rim of Shackleton crater, only 7% of the ground within 1 km is gentler than 10°, so that point should be moved. At another site the nearest ice is 12.3 km away in a straight line, but a rover limited to 15° slopes must drive 28.9 km.

NASA data used

  • LOLA elevation model of the south pole (LRO, NASA GSFC), at 80, 160 and 640 m per pixel: horizon, slope, rover route.
  • SPICE ephemeris DE421 (NASA JPL, NAIF): Sun and Earth positions every hour from 2026 to 2030.
  • Ice detections in permanently shadowed regions from the Moon Mineralogy Mapper (Lemelin et al. 2021): 169 regions.
  • Lunar Prospector iron and thorium maps: estimated rock mix.
  • LRO imagery for the 3D Moon.

Tools, languages and software

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no framework and no build step; drawing with the HTML Canvas.
  • CesiumJS for the 3D Moon, with an automatic fallback to our own 2D maps if it cannot load.
  • Python (with SPICE) and Node.js scripts to prepare the ephemeris, terrain and site data from the NASA sources.
  • Git and GitHub; the site is static files on free hosting, and all computing runs in the visitor’s browser, so there is no server.
  • An AI coding assistant (Claude) was used to write and test a large part of the code and to draft text, under the team’s direction.

What is creative about it

At the pole the Sun does not rise and set; it circles the horizon once every 29.5 days. So the direction of the Sun is the date. The Ring of Light uses this: one circle holds the sky, a month of sunlight, the Earth-contact windows and the lander’s state. We also turn data into a decision: instead of angles, the user gets a verdict and a way out.

What the team considered

  • Honesty about limits: terrain cells are 80 m, so boulders and small craters are not seen; Earth contact is geometric, not a radio link budget; our angles have not yet been compared number by number with JPL Horizons. This is a research and education prototype, not flight certification.
  • Reproducibility: every formula is published in the site’s Guide tab, every dataset is cited, and the scripts that rebuild the data are in the repository.
  • Accessibility: Arabic and English, works in any browser, runs on a phone.
  • Sustainability: zero running cost, simple code that students can maintain.
  • Relation to existing tools: JPL Horizons, Moon Trek and QuickMap offer more precise or richer data; LunarLink_JO complements them by answering the planning question directly.
